title: Ben Shelton successfully defends Canadian Open title in all-American clash
content:
Once the veteran players and most of the top seeds vanished from the Canadian Open, succumbing to injury and upset, the stakes of the tournament in Montreal took on a new edge.

This was the first ATP Masters 1000 event, played at the level just below a Grand Slam, in which all eight quarterfinalists were born in the 2000s. That changed the tenor of the tournament, where suddenly most players weren’t just competing for a prestigious title, but they were also jostling to prove they could lead the pack of the rising generation in men’s tennis — or in Ben Shelton’s case, reiterate the fact he’s already separated himself from his peers.

Shelton’s 6-3, 7-6(4) win over Brandon Nakashima in Thursday’s all-American final fortified Shelton’s spot as far and away the leader of the youth movement in men’s tennis — and showed that the world No. 10 might be righting a topsy-turvy season just in time for the U.S. Open.

It also put him in some fine company. He won his fourth title of the season, and seventh of his career, to join Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz as the third man born in the 2000s to win multiple Masters 1000 titles. He’s the fourth back-to-back Canadian Open champion this century, joining Andy Murray, Novak Djokovic and Rafael Nadal as repeat winners.

In the first all-American final at a Masters 1000 since 2003, he became the third American man this century to win multiple titles at this level alongside Roddick and Andre Agassi.

That’s the type of consistency Shelton has been searching for this season.

On paper, he was always a front-runner in Canada as the defending champion. He was an even stronger pick to win after No. 2 seed Felix Auger-Aliassime withdrew before the first round due to injury, and Alexander Zverev, Alex de Minaur and Daniil Medvedev, the other top seeds, lost early.

But Shelton’s had an odd year at big tournaments. He won three titles — two at 500-level events and one at a 250-level event — but logged a second-round loss at the French Open and a stunning first-round loss at Wimbledon.

Before last week in Montreal, he had notched exactly one win at a Masters 1000 tournament this year, and it was in March at Indian Wells.

Shelton couldn’t quite piece together a pattern in the losses, but he had theories. He relishes a big match and can fall into a trap of overlooking early-round matches, was one. Another is that he’s a rhythm guy who feels his best when he plays every day, which he doesn’t at Grand Slams and Masters 1000 tournaments. He also hadn’t been returning as well as he would have liked.

But as frustrating as the early-round losses were, Shelton felt he was still ticking enough boxes — playing well in those matches and doing the right thing in practice, chiefly — that he could dismiss the poor results as flukes.

In Canada, with the U.S. Open just weeks away, it was time for Shelton to lock in. The courts played slow, meaning his cracking serve was ultra-effective. With many of the top seeds falling early, the draw opened up. All Shelton had to do was stay steady and take advantage.

He did more than that, dominating a less-established field (the highest-ranked player he beat was No. 17 Jakub Menšík) as he should, without dropping a set. His serve and forehand were on point, but most importantly, his returns were effective.

He entered Thursday’s final with a 5-0 record against Nakashima, who played the most confident tennis of his career to reach his first Masters 1000 final.

The 25-year-old from California opened the final with some swagger, popping four aces in the first game, but his self-assurance quickly ebbed. Serving at 3-3 in the first set, he faced triple break point and showed brief flashes of the type of play that got him to the final by hitting another ace and then becoming a backboard against Shelton’s forceful groundstrokes to make it 30-40.

But in the first swing of the match, Nakashima botched his first serve, and on his second, Shelton sent a booming, 97 mph lefty forehand down the line that curled into the court to earn him the break.

Shelton cruised from there, mixing his primary weapons in with athletic defense that garnered big reactions from the Montreal crowd and deflated Nakashima even more. Nakashima, who had not reached a quarterfinal at a Masters 1000 before this event, pushed Shelton at the end of the second set, but his charge proved too late.
